title: One-shot ferroelectric shadow freezes rows before charge leaks
idea: Time-shift between two storage physics: the capacitor stack has a thin HZO layer left untouched during DRAM-speed use, and when a row's age counter passes ~half its retention one pulse copies the charge state into polarization, after which charge may leak freely; the next read senses polarization switching current and returns the row to charge mode.
why: No periodic refresh (fact 3), and FE endurance is spent only once per long idle episode, sidestepping FeRAM's endurance limit.

title: Leak-to-archive cells write their own nonvolatile backup
idea: Time-shift the leak into a write: each cell's leakage path runs through a tiny ionic memristive integrator, so the charge draining from a stored '1' over seconds moves ions and leaves a resistance state recording it; after full decay the sense amp reads the memristor instead, and the next write resets it.
why: The leaking energy itself writes the backup, so refresh power is zero (fact 3); memristor reset endurance is the main risk.

title: Keyed Feistel scrambler in decoder randomizes physical row adjacency
idea: Substitute the fixed logical-to-physical row map with a tiny keyed Feistel permutation in the row predecoder, re-keyed each refresh epoch with background migration, so attackers cannot know which physical rows neighbor their aggressors.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): defeats targeted many-sided hammering at a few hundred gates per bank instead of large counter tables.

title: Analog-voltage address bus with per-row window comparators
idea: Substitute the binary multi-wire address bus with two analog address lines (row-group and row-within-group voltages); each wordline driver carries a resistor-ladder window comparator that fires only when both voltages land in its window, which is coincidence decoding in the analog domain.
why: Periphery area: replaces ~16 address wires and NAND trees with 2 lines plus local comparators, simplifying routing in narrow sub-array gaps.

title: Coincident dual-gate matrix wordline addressing cuts drivers to 2sqrtN
idea: Decoding a row needs only log2(N) bits of information, yet DRAM spends one 3 V driver per row. Use a dual-gate access transistor whose front gate is a row-group line and back gate a sub-row line; it conducts only when both are high, so 1024 rows need 32+32 drivers instead of 1024 (display-style matrix addressing inside the mat).
why: Periphery area (fact 7): sub-wordline driver strips shrink ~10x, ~8-12% die area recovered; fewer high-voltage devices.

title: Time-to-latch sensing rescues Z-RAM floating-body margin
idea: Failure mined: Innovative Silicon's Z-RAM read the parasitic bipolar current of a floating body, and the 0/1 current difference shrank below sense-amp offset at 32 nm. Fix: read the delay until the parasitic BJT latches under a fixed bias ramp. That delay depends exponentially on stored body charge, and a time-to-digital converter shared by 16 bitlines digitizes it.
why: Turns a few-uA current difference into a multi-ns timing difference (~10x effective margin). That makes capacitorless cells (no 70:1 capacitor, fact 1) readable at scaled nodes, and sharing the TDC keeps periphery small.

title: Self-referenced two-pulse sensing eliminates reference bitlines
idea: Substitute the external reference (dummy cell or VDD/2 twin bitline) with the cell itself: read once, inject a known small charge step into the same cell, read again, and let the sign of the difference give the data. This is the self-reference trick from MRAM applied to DRAM.
why: Density: makes open-bitline, near-4F^2 layouts tolerable without reference-mismatch errors, gaining ~1.3-1.5x cell density.

title: tRCD-sweep charge spectroscopy predicts per-row retention in seconds
idea: Effect: RC kinetics of charge sharing. A small team's FPGA DDR5 controller reads each row repeatedly while shortening tRCD in 0.5 ns steps; the step where bits flip shows how far the stored charge sits from the sense trip point after a known wait. Fitting the decay gives each row's leakage rate without hour-long pauses, and rows are binned into 64/128/256/512 ms refresh classes.
why: Refresh (fact 3): multi-rate refresh can cut refresh operations ~60-75%, and profiling drops from hours to seconds per DIMM, so it can run in the field.

title: Movable-type periphery: reusable pre-tested sense/decoder tiles across array generations
idea: Like Gutenberg's reusable type sorts, cast a library of periphery tiles (sense-amp strips, sub-wordline driver strips, pump and I/O tiles) on a depreciated logic wafer, test them, and hybrid-bond known-good tiles under each new array die. When the array shrinks, only a thin bitline-pitch adapter layer is re-cut; the tile library is reused for 3-4 array generations.
why: Periphery (~49% of die) is redesigned and re-fabbed on the expensive DRAM node every generation; reusable tiles cut DRAM-node wafer area per bit ~35-45% and periphery mask/NRE cost ~70%.

title: Coincident X-Y selection with dual-gate access transistor
idea: Like core memory's coincident-current selection, give each access transistor two gates (row wordline plus a column-segment select line) so only cells where both are high open; activating a cache line opens 64-512 cells, not an 8 kb row.
why: Overfetch (fact 8) and row hammer (fact 9): removes most of the 128x overfetch (~5.9 pJ to under 1 pJ per useful bit) and confines hammer exposure to a segment.

title: Core-memory coincident selection shrinks decoders and overfetch
idea: Borrowed from magnetic core memory's coincident-current addressing: each cell has two series access transistors, one gated by an X line and one by a Y line, so only the intersection is selected. A mat needs 2*sqrt(N) drivers, and one Y line opens just a 64-bit segment.
why: Periphery and overfetch (facts 7, 8): driver count per mat down ~30x and activation granularity ~128x finer, cutting random-read energy per useful bit ~5x.

title: Victim-margin metering: measure hammered neighbors instead of counting aggressors
idea: Reverse row-hammer defense: on a random 1-in-64 activation, the SA strip re-senses the two neighbor rows with a reference shifted by ~30 mV; only if a bit fails the shifted reference (margin eroded) is that victim refreshed, so no per-row activation counters exist.
why: Fact 9: removes per-bank counter SRAM/CAM tables (several % of periphery) and refreshes only truly degraded victims, robust even at ~1k-activation thresholds.

title: Thyristor latch wordline drivers from one implant
idea: Revive the thyratron, in its SCR form, as a wordline driver. One added implant mask forms a PNPN stack at each sub-wordline end. A tiny decoder pulse triggers it, it latches the wordline high from a pulsed 3 V rail, and it resets when the rail drops at precharge, so no level shifter or large thick-oxide PMOS is needed.
why: Sub-wordline driver stripes, a major periphery block, shrink ~2-3x (fact 7) and level shifters disappear (fact 10).

title: Ovonic-threshold-switch crosspoint replaces per-row wordline driver selection
idea: Effect: ovonic threshold switching. Select wordlines through a BEOL crosspoint of OTS devices: a group line at +V/2 and an index line at -V/2 exceed the OTS threshold (~1.5 V) only at their intersection, which snaps on and charges that wordline. This is coincident selection, as in core memory, done with threshold switching; N drivers become ~2*sqrt(N).
why: Periphery area (fact 7): ~16x fewer driver transistors per sub-wordline strip for 1024 rows.

title: Perfecting-press wafer: periphery printed on the backside of the array
idea: Like a perfecting press that prints both sides of a sheet in one pass, thin the finished array wafer to ~1 um and build low-temperature periphery transistors (laser-annealed Si or oxide FETs) on its backside. These connect to bitlines and wordlines through sub-um nano-TSVs directly beneath each mat.
why: Periphery stops consuming front-side area: array efficiency rises from ~51% to ~85%, ~1.6x bits per wafer without a litho shrink, and SA-to-bitline paths get shorter.

title: Back-gate the array so wordlines swing at logic voltage
idea: Reverse which terminal does the work: a buried, separately biased plate under the access transistors sits negative during retention (raising Vt, cutting leakage) and pulses positive only in the selected subarray, so wordlines need ~1.2 V swing instead of ~3 V and drivers become thin-oxide core devices.
why: Facts 10, 7 and 3: wordline driver area -50-60%, wordline CV^2 energy ~-80%, VPP pump removed; deeper retention bias trims the leakage tail.

title: Telegraph-style regenerative repeaters halve effective bitline capacitance
idea: Undersea telegraph cables used repeaters to regenerate signals along long spans; a 4-transistor regenerative latch at each bitline's midpoint isolates the far segment, amplifies the near-segment signal, then drives the far segment, so each cell sees half the bitline capacitance.
why: Doubles cells per SA or doubles signal, so relaxed-pitch DUV arrays stay viable with 2x longer bitlines (facts 1, 7).

title: Springfield Armory standard: public-domain 180 nm periphery masks for U.S. fabs
idea: Like the Springfield Armory's government-owned gauges that made interchangeable parts possible, a federal program funds and publishes an open periphery reference design, bump map and mask set at 180 nm. Any U.S. 200 mm fab can then make certified companion dies that bond to any compliant array die.
why: Removes periphery NRE (~$50-100M per product) as a barrier for new U.S. entrants and creates interchangeable second-source supply.

title: Flash translation layer remaps bad rows outside the die
idea: Borrowed from NAND SSD bad-block management: DRAM dies ship with no redundant rows, fuse banks or address comparators; the memory controller loads a per-die bad-row map from SPD and remaps addresses into a pooled spare region.
why: Periphery: deletes ~3-5% of die area (spares, fuses, compare logic) and pools spares across dies, raising effective yield.

title: Resonant adiabatic wordline drive, reversible computing's missing killer app
idea: Failure mined: adiabatic and reversible logic (MIT, Younis) died because irregular logic needed multi-phase resonant power clocks. DRAM is the opposite case: wordlines and bitlines are large, regular capacitive loads switched on a periodic tRC beat. Fix: drive them from shared LC tanks with inductors in the package substrate, swinging to 3 V and back while recovering the charge.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): recovers 60-80% of wordline and bitline CV^2 energy, cutting activation energy ~2-3x without lowering any voltage.

title: Zn: zinc-oxide acoustic resonator replaces the DLL clock
idea: Fabricate a ZnO film bulk acoustic resonator, with ZnO grown hydrothermally or by O2-only reactive sputtering rather than argon sputtering, on the periphery as a low-jitter GHz reference so the DQ path uses a small injection-locked oscillator instead of a large DLL.
why: DLLs and clock trees burn standby power and area; ~1-2% die area and ~10% I/O idle power saved (facts 5, 7).

title: Stepwise tank-capacitor bitline charging cuts precharge energy several-fold
idea: Effect: adiabatic stepwise charging. In a small team's MPW macro, bitlines charge and discharge through 3-4 intermediate voltage steps supplied by on-die tank capacitors, so each step dissipates only ~C(V/N)^2; the tanks self-balance because rising and falling lines exchange charge through them.
why: Energy per bit (facts 8, 10): bitline CV^2 energy falls ~N-fold (2-3x in practice) without lowering VARY, at the cost of ~1-2 ns per step.

title: Minify sense-amp count: one amplifier serially resolves eight held bitlines
idea: MINIFY the SA population 8x: bitlines are left floating after charge sharing (they hold the signal for ~100 ns as their own capacitors), and an 8:1 analog mux steps one larger, low-offset SA across them, each resolve-and-restore taking ~3 ns.
why: Fact 7 (periphery ~49%): SA stripe area -60-70%, periphery share toward ~40%; the larger shared SA also has lower offset; cost is ~20 ns longer row cycle.

title: Co-aging reference cell that leaks in lockstep with data
idea: Worse: compare every leaking cell against a fixed VDD/2 reference so margin shrinks every millisecond. Flip: each row carries a few reference cells written to a half level at the same instant as the data, through identical access transistors, so the reference droops with the data and the sense amp compares against a co-aged threshold.
why: Leakage tail forcing refresh (fact 3): most '1' margin loss is common-mode droop; tracking it could stretch retention 2-4x and cut refresh energy and bandwidth loss ~50-75%.

title: Impressionist painting: low-swing lossy sensing for low-order bit planes
idea: An impressionist painting only needs the broad strokes right. Store AI tensors so the low-order bit planes live in dedicated mats that run at VARY ~0.4 V and short sense times with an allowed raw bit error rate of ~1e-4, while sign and exponent planes run at full margin with ECC.
why: ~6x less CV2 energy on the 50-75% of bits that are low-order, about 10x on those mats, with negligible model-accuracy loss from LSB flips; a precision-aware access mode is needed in the controller.

title: Two-bit-per-cell DRAM with Gray-coded four-level sensing
idea: Box: high-k pillar cap x Si access x 4-level successive-approximation sensing x standard x bulk Si x standard. Each cell stores one of four charge levels read by a 2-step SAR comparator; Gray mapping makes most level errors single-bit, so the ~1% raw error rate fits a rate-0.88 code.
why: Density: 2 bits per cell gives ~1.75x bits per mm^2 after parity, with no new lithography.

title: Erasure-flagging sense amps: weak decisions marked, not guessed
idea: Limit: accept a raw bit error rate of 1e-4. A second, time-delayed sample in each SA flags bits that resolved slowly (small |dV|) as erasures, and a short per-burst erasure code corrects up to 4 flagged bits per 64 B with little overhead, since known-location errors cost half the parity.
why: Sense margin: tolerating 1e-4 lets Cs shrink ~30% or refresh intervals lengthen 2-4x (facts 1, 3), with soft information borrowed from NAND applied to DRAM.

title: Eliminate CMOS sense latches: resonant-tunneling-diode Goto pairs
idea: Two series resonant tunneling diodes (SiGe/Si or InGaAs, grown on the bonded periphery die) form a MOBILE/Goto-pair bistable whose midpoint ties to the bitline. When the shared clocked bias rises, the pair snaps in ~10 ps to the state set by the bitline imbalance, and the same NDR logic can do column muxing.
why: Replaces 4-6 MOSFETs with 2 RTDs (SA area -50%, sensing ~10x faster), attacking the periphery share (fact 7). Integrating RTDs and keeping their peak current uniform is hard.

title: P: phosphorus-doped Esaki diode Goto pair as sense latch
idea: Use two degenerately doped silicon tunnel diodes (P and B gas-phase doping in H2, no argon-diluted implanter source) in series as a Goto pair on the bitline; the negative-resistance pair has two stable states and resolves a few-mV imbalance in tens of ps at ~0.3 V.
why: Breaks the ~1 V sensing floor (fact 10) and replaces a 4-6 transistor latch with two diodes; claims ~5x lower sensing energy.

title: Pilot-tone automatic gain control lowers array voltage
idea: Like the AGC in 1930s tube radios: each activation also reads two pilot cells (a known 1 and a known 0) on dedicated bitlines, and their sensed amplitude sets the main sense amps' latch-enable delay and reference trim in real time. Margin tracks temperature and aging directly, so VARY can drop from ~1.0 V toward 0.7 V without worst-case guardbands.
why: Attacks the voltage floor (fact 10): CV² array energy falls ~50% at 0.7 V, for 2 extra bitlines per ~1k.

title: Integrate-and-fire latency-code sensing with one shared comparator per 16 bitlines
idea: Like a neuron's latency code, each bitline discharges into a 2-transistor integrate-and-fire node whose firing time encodes stored charge, and 16 bitlines share one arbitrated time-to-digital comparator. A one-transistor restore pull per bitline is driven from the decoded result.
why: Fact 7: replaces a ~10-transistor cross-coupled sense amp per pair with ~3 small devices plus a shared TDC. Sense-amp area falls ~50-60%, about 8-10% of the die.

title: Van der Waals resonant-tunneling pairs make each node bistable
idea: Atomic-layer scale jump: two stacked graphene/hBN resonant-tunneling diodes on each storage node form a Goto pair, so the node latches statically at either rail with valley current engineered below 1 fA; data never decays, so there is no refresh cycle at all.
why: Zero refresh power and bandwidth (fact 3), with hold current below the ~1 fA refresh-equivalent; scaling the vdW RTD peak-to-valley ratio is the risk.

title: Fly-by-wire wordlines: per-mat VPP trimmed to the minimum
idea: A fly-by-wire jet trims each control surface on its own. Each mat gets a small LDO that drops its wordline high level from global VPP to the lowest value that passed that mat's test margin, stored in fuses.
why: Typical mats run 10-15% below worst-case VPP, cutting wordline energy ~20-25% and reducing GIDL and hammer coupling (facts 9, 10).

title: Eliminate refresh logic and wordline segmentation in a 77 K memory tier
idea: Run a liquid-nitrogen-cooled DRAM tier at 77 K, where access-transistor leakage collapses (retention of hours) and copper resistivity drops ~7x. That permits deleting the refresh controller, the sub-wordline driver stripes (4x longer wordlines) and half of the SA stripes (lower noise and mismatch).
why: Facts 3 and 7: removes refresh power and bandwidth loss, and the periphery area falls ~10-15%; LN2 cooling energy is partly offset by lower I/O resistance.

title: Lizard-tail autotomy: salvaging fab-reject dies by amputating failed mats
idea: Lizards shed a tail to survive. Buy DRAM dies that fail final test on a few unrepairable mats or a dead sense-amp stripe, map those regions out with post-package repair plus a controller remap table, and sell them as odd-capacity modules (e.g., 14 GB) for caching tiers. $1M covers a used-tester test flow and first lots within 24 months.
why: Supply axis: turns several % of yield fallout into sellable bits at a fraction of new cost/bit, with no fab capex.

title: Eliminate probe pads and probe cards: optically powered contactless wafer test
idea: Give each die a 100 um coil and a small photovoltaic cell. Flood illumination powers whole wafers, and test patterns flow over near-field inductive links at ~1 Gb/s, so thousands of dies test in parallel untouched. Probe pads, their drivers and test-lane ESD disappear.
why: Test is ~8-12% of DRAM cost; massively parallel contactless test lifts tester throughput ~10x and frees ~1-2% of die area.

title: Column-gated local wordline drivers activate one-eighth rows
idea: AND each sub-wordline driver enable with a column-segment signal decoded from the column address, so an ACT opens only the ~1 kb segment holding the requested data; the gate fits in existing SWD strips on old processes.
why: Overfetch (fact 8): ~5-8x lower activation energy per random access, and ~8x less hammer coupling per activate (fact 9).

title: Minify the page: 512-bit sense slices with local wordline drivers
idea: MINIFY the activated page from 8 Kb to 512 bits: split each master wordline with local wordline drivers every 512 cells and gate sense-amp enable per slice using column address bits sent with ACT, so only the needed slice is charge-shared, sensed and restored.
why: Fact 8 (128x overfetch, ~5.9 pJ per useful bit): activation energy per useful bit drops ~10x and fewer bitlines swing near victims; cost ~3-4% area for extra local drivers.

title: Column-first activation: CAS before RAS opens one row segment
idea: Reverse the RAS-then-CAS order: the column address arrives first and enables only the sub-wordline drivers and local SAs of the 1/16 row segment containing it, so ~512 bits are activated, sensed and restored instead of 8 Kb.
why: Fact 8 (128x overfetch): activation energy per useful bit ~5.9 pJ -> ~0.6 pJ; unopened segments also escape row-hammer stress. Costs ~3% area for segment-enable gating.

title: Spare array mats double as flying capacitors for wordline charge pumps
idea: Box: pillar caps x array access FETs as switches x no sensing x in-array power conversion x bulk Si x zero added masks. A few mats per bank wire their millions of 5 fF cell caps into parallel groups clocked as a switched-capacitor VPP/VBB pump, replacing the large planar MOS pump capacitors in the periphery.
why: Pump and decap area (several % of die) shrinks ~80% because cell caps are ~100x denser than MOS caps.

title: Capacitance-collapse bitline boost from one varactor implant
idea: Echoing 1950s varactor parametric amplifiers, each bitline gets a strip of MOS varactor, formed by one added accumulation-well implant mask, held in its high-capacitance state during charge sharing. Just before latching it is switched to depletion, roughly halving total bitline capacitance, so with charge conserved the differential voltage about doubles with no transistor noise.
why: Doubles sense signal (facts 1, 8), allowing ~2x smaller Cs or 2x longer bitlines with half the sense stripes (fact 7).

title: Spin-Hall nonvolatile shadow latches let periphery power-gate between accesses
idea: Effect: spin Hall effect (spin-orbit torque). Pair each sense amp with a three-terminal SOT-MTJ on a beta-Ta strip (no tungsten) that copies the latched row in ~1 ns; idle banks cut power to SA and periphery stripes and reopen the row from the shadow copy without a new activation.
why: Idle power and row hammer (fact 9): periphery leakage in idle banks drops ~50-80%, and fewer re-activations lower hammer exposure.

title: Skyrmion bubble memory: globally clocked major/minor loops, TMR detectors
idea: Failure mined: magnetic bubble memory (TI, Intel Magnetics) died on micron-size bubbles, 100 kHz shifting and millivolt permalloy detectors. Fix: keep its best idea, one global drive that clocks every loop at once with no per-bit transistors, but use 25 nm skyrmions in Co/Pt multilayers pushed by a global spin-orbit current sheet. Data is read through block-replicate gates onto a major loop with one 200% TMR detector per 4096 bits.
why: 10x at the same cost: ~60 nm^2 per bit vs ~860 nm^2 per DRAM cell, with periphery amortized over 4k bits. The films are blanket sputtered layers with ~2 critical masks, no capacitors and no EUV.

title: Leaky-capacitor analog activation counter per row stops row hammer
idea: MINIFY the row-hammer tracker from multi-KB SRAM count tables to ~2 transistors and one tiny capacitor per wordline driver: each ACT pumps in a fixed charge packet, a calibrated leak drains it with a ~64 ms time constant, and crossing threshold raises a neighbor-refresh request.
why: Fact 9 (flips at ~1k activations): exact per-row tracking for ~1% periphery area instead of probabilistic sampling, with no counter SRAM.

title: Two-transistor analog charge integrators count activations per wordline
idea: Worse: let rows be hammered with zero memory of past activations. Flip: every local wordline driver deposits a fixed charge packet on a per-row leaky MOS integrator at each activation; a shared comparator in the driver strip samples it on activation and fires neighbor refresh when it crosses threshold, while the leak resets it naturally each window.
why: Row hammer at ~1k activations (fact 9): per-row tracking for every row in ~2-3 transistors instead of SRAM counter tables.

title: Mg: MgO magnetic-junction coin-flippers drive randomized row-hammer refresh
idea: Use the thermally stochastic switching of low-barrier MgO tunnel junctions as a true random bit source in every bank, so each ACT triggers a neighbor refresh with tunable probability p, with no LFSRs, counters or tables.
why: Probabilistic row-hammer defenses need fast, unbiased, attack-proof randomness; one ~0.01 um2 MTJ per bank replaces counter tables, cutting row-hammer logic area >10x at ~1k thresholds (fact 9).

title: Laser-trimmed op-amp offset trim for minimum-size sense amps
idea: Borrowed from precision analog trimming: sense-amp transistors are drawn at minimum size (accepting large mismatch), and each SA gets a 3-bit trim capacitor array whose code is measured by power-up BIST and held in a small nonvolatile register per 8 SAs. Matching comes from digital trim instead of area.
why: Periphery ~49% (fact 7): sense-amp stripe area down ~2.5-3x; stripes are ~10-15% of the die, so ~6-8% die per bit is saved.

title: Bond-wire inductive boost converter generates wordline voltage without charge pump
idea: Effect: inductive flyback (L di/dt). Use the package's existing bond-wire inductance (~1-2 nH per wire, several in parallel) as the inductor of an on-die switched boost converter at ~0.5-1 GHz, generating VPP at ~70% efficiency instead of a ~30%-efficient multi-stage capacitive pump.
why: Periphery area/energy (facts 7, 10): VPP generator area ~-60% and energy ~-50%, using only standard wire bonding and MPW CMOS.

title: Periodic action: resonant LC wordline drive recycles boost energy
idea: TRIZ #19 Periodic action: wordlines are driven from a resonant tank formed by an interposer inductor and the selected wordline capacitance, so the ~3 V boost arrives as a half-sine and its charge returns to the tank when the wordline falls, bypassing most of the ~30%-efficient VPP charge pump.
why: Fact 10: wordline/VPP energy ~-60% and charge-pump area in the periphery ~-50%.

title: Stepwise tank-capacitor charging cuts wordline drive energy
idea: Ideal result: wordlines that swing 3 V for free. Drive each global wordline through 4-6 staircase steps from on-die tank capacitors at intermediate voltages, so each step dissipates only (dV)^2 and charge returns to the tanks on the falling edge.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): wordline swing energy drops ~3-5x and charge pump load falls accordingly.

title: Laser-crystallized poly-Si repeaters amplify bitlines every 32 cells
idea: Substitute one long passive bitline feeding one end latch with a distributed bitline: excimer-laser-crystallized poly-Si TFT repeater stages every 32 cells regenerate the charge-shared signal locally, as display backplanes do.
why: Charge wall: each segment sees only 32 cells of bitline capacitance, giving ~8x higher signal per femtofarad and allowing much smaller Cs.

title: Selectron-style binary-coded tier selection replaces the 3D DRAM staircase
idea: Failure mined: RCA's Selectron tube picked one of 256 storage spots with combinations of a few grid bars, a decoder built into the medium, and died on vacuum-tube complexity. Fix: in a 3D DRAM stack, each tier's cells sit behind log2(N) series select gates whose thresholds are set by log2(N) masked implants, so 6 shared vertical gate lines decode 64 tiers. Staircase contacts and per-tier wordline drivers disappear.
why: 10x at the same cost: periphery and staircase area stay nearly flat as tiers grow (log N, not N), which moves 3D DRAM break-even from ~26 tiers to ~8 (fact 2) and makes 64-128 tiers ~10x denser at near-3D-NAND cost per mm^2.

title: Miura-fold bitlines: true and complement stacked vertically, not side by side
idea: Fold the bitline pair like Miura-ori: the true bitline runs on tier 1 and its complement directly above on tier 2, swapping tiers every 64 cells through a zig-zag via 'crease'. Both lines see identical wordline and neighbor coupling, giving folded-bitline noise rejection in the lateral footprint of an open bitline.
why: Open-bitline cell density with folded-bitline common-mode immunity, and each sense amp gets 2x the lateral pitch; ~30% less signal margin needed and an easier SA-pitch wall.

title: Self-boosting gain cell drives a plain inverter, no sense amp
idea: $1 IoT chips cannot afford precision analog: a 3T gain cell whose read wordline couples its storage node upward yields a near-rail bitline swing, so a skewed inverter replaces the cross-coupled SA and reference generator, all drawn at relaxed DUV rules.
why: SA area -70% and no offset trimming; periphery simple enough for 40-90 nm U.S. fabs, trading some cell area.

title: Triage-nurse refresh: in-die retention classes skip strong rows
idea: A triage nurse checks the sickest patients most often. At wafer test each row's retention is classed by timed SA reads after reduced restore; the class map sits in a small on-die table, and the internal refresh engine skips strong rows on most REF commands, with a guard class for variable-retention cells.
why: Cuts internal refresh operations ~50-70% and their energy (fact 3) while REF commands stay unchanged.

title: Eliminate half the sense-amp stripes with decomposable-polymer air-gap bitlines
idea: Pattern bitlines with Cl-based etch, fill between them with polynorbornene (a fluorine-free sacrificial polymer, patterned in O2), cap with TEOS oxide, and decompose the polymer at ~400 C. The air gaps cut bitline capacitance ~35%, so bitlines can be ~1.6x longer per SA and roughly every other SA stripe is deleted.
why: Removes ~5-6% of die area in SA stripes, or alternatively gives +50% signal to ease the Cs wall (fact 1).

title: Resonant gate drive recovers wordline CV-squared energy
idea: Borrowed from resonant gate drivers in MHz power converters: groups of wordline drivers share an LC tank (inductor in the package or interposer), so each wordline charges along a sinusoid and its charge returns to the tank on close instead of being dumped to ground.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): recovers ~50-70% of the ~3 V wordline swing energy and shrinks the VPP charge pump that feeds it.

title: Ti: titanium-oxide BEOL ROM stores per-row retention class
idea: At wafer test, measure every row's retention and write a 2-bit class into a TiOx resistive crosspoint ROM printed above the row decoder; the refresh counter reads the class inline and refreshes strong rows at 128-512 ms instead of 32-64 ms.
why: The leakage tail forces worst-case refresh (fact 3); multi-rate refresh cuts refresh operations ~70-80%, recovering 10-20% bandwidth and much of idle power with ~zero silicon area.

title: Dithered stochastic-resonance voting for weak, leaky cells
idea: Inverting 'noise must be suppressed': during refresh and retry reads a small auxiliary comparator samples the held bitline 8 times with an injected calibrated dither and majority-votes, then forces the main latch, so cells left with only ~1/3 of nominal charge still read correctly.
why: Lets refresh intervals roughly double (refresh energy -50%, refresh is 16-33% of idle power) by tolerating deeper charge loss in the leakage tail.

title: Pyroelectric HZO film senses per-mat heating for mat-level refresh scaling
idea: Effect: pyroelectricity. Deposit a 10 nm Si-doped HfO2 pyroelectric capacitor (same ALD as HZO) beside each mat; temperature change yields charge dQ = p*A*dT with no bias power, integrated by a shared ADC and periodically re-zeroed against one diode sensor. Refresh rate is then set per mat instead of by the hottest on-die sensor.
why: Refresh (fact 3): retention roughly doubles per ~10 C, so mats 10-15 C cooler than the hotspot can refresh 2-3x less often, cutting refresh energy ~30-40% on unevenly heated dies.

title: Magnify sense time: integrating time-to-digital sensing for 1.5 fF cells
idea: MAGNIFY the sensing window from ~2 ns to 20-40 ns: after charge sharing, a constant-current integrator per bitline pair races both lines to a threshold and a shared counter (TDC) records which crosses first and by how much, resolving 5-10 mV differences a latch cannot.
why: Fact 1: tolerating ~3x less signal lets Cs fall from ~5 fF to ~1.5 fF, so pillar AR can fall from ~70:1 to ~25:1; added latency is hidden behind a row-buffer/SRAM tier for hot data.

title: Field-emission display tips become vacuum-channel sense amplifiers
idea: Borrowed from field-emission displays' nanogap emitters on glass: nanoscale vacuum-channel transistors (sub-100 nm gaps, which work in air below the electron mean free path) serve as sense-amp input pairs whose transconductance does not depend on substrate crystal quality.
why: Gives glass substrates fast, high-gain sensing despite poor thin-film mobility, and is radiation-hard; a speculative path to periphery without silicon.

title: Ant-colony optimizer for spare row and column repair allocation
idea: Ants find short paths with depositing and evaporating pheromone. Ant-colony optimization solves the NP-hard redundancy-allocation problem (which spares fix a fail bitmap) on tester-side GPUs, approaching optimal repair. Two engineers plus partner fail bitmaps, ~$500k in 24 months.
why: Fact 7: spares, fuses and compare logic are several % of the die. Equal repair with ~25% fewer spares, or +1-3% repair yield on today's spares, cuts cost/bit directly.

title: Dekatron token ring scans refresh with no counter or decoder
idea: Dekatron counting tubes moved a glow one cathode per pulse. Thread a one-hot token through a 2-transistor dynamic shift chain built into the sub-wordline driver stripe, like an LCD gate driver. Each refresh pulse fires the token's row and passes the token on, so refresh needs no address counter, no internal address mux and no decoder toggling. Zero masks added.
why: Cuts refresh energy ~20-30% by not toggling decoder trees (fact 3) and removes refresh-address logic (fact 7).

title: Vinyl record pressing: nanoimprint all periphery-only layers
idea: Like pressing vinyl from a master stamper, pattern periphery-only layers (implant blocks, periphery contacts, metals at >=40 nm half-pitch) by jet-and-flash nanoimprint: drop-dispensed UV resist, imprint, cure, and descum the residual layer by plasma. No wet develop, no BARC rinse, no EUV.
why: Water: each periphery litho module loses its develop/rinse (~10x less UPW per layer); litho capital per periphery layer is ~3-5x lower.

title: Jet-and-flash nanoimprint patterns all relaxed-pitch periphery layers
idea: Worse: expose even relaxed periphery metal layers on immersion or EUV scanners at full scanner capex. Flip: print periphery interconnect and contact layers with jet-and-flash nanoimprint templates, reserving scanners for array-critical layers.
why: Capital intensity (fact 4): nanoimprint tools cost ~1/3-1/5 of a scanner per layer and use far less power.

title: LN2 memory pods with 4x wordlines and 2x bitlines
idea: Design a die only for 77 K immersion pods: copper resistivity drops ~6x so each sub-wordline driver can serve 4x more cells, and lower thermal noise plus near-zero leakage allow 2x longer bitlines with a longer sense window. SWD and SA stripes shrink to roughly a third of their usual area.
why: Periphery 49% -> ~25-30% of die, refresh eliminated (fact 3), ~1.4x bits per wafer; cost moves into cryo infrastructure.

title: OTDR reflectometry reads a whole column from one pulse
idea: Borrowed from optical time-domain reflectometers: a glass-panel bitline is built as a low-loss transmission line, each cell's state switches a small shunt impedance, and a ~20 ps pulse launched from one end returns reflections whose timing gives cell position and whose amplitude gives state.
why: Periphery: one fast receiver reads hundreds of cells per pulse instead of hundreds of sense amps; only practical on low-loss glass with centimeter lines.

title: LCD polarity inversion cancels oxide-TFT bias stress
idea: Borrowed from LCD dot inversion, which keeps liquid crystal from DC drift: the periphery stores each row inverted on alternate refresh epochs, tracked by a per-row polarity bit, so IGZO access and sense transistors see near-zero average bias stress.
why: Removes oxide-TFT threshold drift (often 100+ mV over life) from the sensing budget, so glass-panel sense amps can run tighter margins for longer.

title: Battery coulomb-counting: dual-threshold reads flag weakening rows
idea: Like a battery gauge estimating health on every cycle, each SA gets a second small comparator at a raised '1' threshold; normal reads flag cells that have lost >40% of charge, and the row goes into a per-bank weak-row table refreshed at 4x while all other rows refresh at 1/4 rate.
why: Refresh (46 fJ/bit, 16-33% of idle power): ~60-70% fewer refreshes, driven by live in-field retention data instead of one-time profiling.

title: Inductive coil links replace TSVs in trailing-node stacks
idea: Stack 8 trailing-node DRAM dies with no TSVs: data and commands move vertically through on-chip coils drawn in existing top-metal layers (ThruChip-style inductive coupling), while power arrives through staircase wire bonds at OSATs.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): avoids TSV processing and its ~20-30% yield loss, giving ~1 Tb/s stacked bandwidth from legacy fabs plus wire-bond capacity.

title: Single-electron electrometer sense amps make 300-electron cells readable
idea: Failure mined: Hitachi's room-temperature single-electron memory (Yano) died because the SET was too variable as a storage device. Fix: use the SET only as the sensor, a 3 nm silicon-island electrometer per 32-cell local bitline with charge sensitivity near 0.01 e, auto-calibrated on every access. Cells then need only ~300 electrons (~0.05 fF), which planar thin-film storage nodes can hold.
why: 10x at the same cost: a 100x smaller capacitor removes the 70:1 pillar and allows a 3D-NAND-style stack of 32+ tiers of lateral planar cells from deposited layers, ~10x bits/mm^2 at similar litho cost.

title: Noise-cancelling headphones: cross-neutralization capacitors cancel bitline coupling
idea: Like active noise cancellation, inject anti-noise: each SA gets small neutralization capacitors from both neighbours' complementary latch nodes, so as an adjacent bitline develops its signal, an equal anti-phase charge is injected, nulling bitline-to-bitline coupling at 24 nm pitch.
why: Signal margin (fact 1): coupling from opposite-data neighbours steals ~20-30% of read signal; recovering it is worth ~1 fF of Cs or ~25% longer bitlines with fewer SA strips.

title: Refresh stream doubles as a free read channel
idea: Ideal result: reading costs nothing because the row is already open. Route rows opened by refresh into an on-die staging buffer and serve queued reads to that row from it, while the scheduler reorders refresh to hit predicted hot rows first.
why: Refresh and destructive read (facts 3, 8): turns part of the 10-20% refresh bandwidth loss into useful bandwidth, up to ~10% effective gain.

title: Second-harmonic phase sensing reads ferroelectric bits without switching them
idea: Constraint: bits must survive power loss and reads must not wear the cell. Store data as HZO polarization but never switch it to read: a 100 mV, ~1 GHz sinusoid on the plate yields a second-harmonic bitline current whose phase flips with polarization direction (dielectric nonlinearity is odd in P), and a per-column mixer clocked from the same plate tone integrates ~5 ns and latches the sign.
why: Non-volatile with a non-destructive read: no write-back (fact 8), no refresh (fact 3), and read endurance effectively unlimited, since wear happens only on writes.

title: Solvent-releasable spare-die patch site on every DIMM
idea: Ideal result: a module that repairs itself by accepting a spare part. Each DIMM has an empty die site using anisotropic conductive film; when a die fails, a depot bonds a spare there and the register clock driver remaps that die's chip-select to it, and the film later dissolves for reclaim.
why: Usable supply: keeps 95%+ of module bits in service instead of scrapping whole DIMMs during a shortage.

title: Magnetosome-chain anisotropic interconnect joining periphery wafer to array wafer
idea: Magnetotactic bacteria align magnetite crystals into chains. Fill a bonding dielectric with Fe3O4/Ni nanoparticles and cure it under a vertical magnetic field, so conductive pillar chains self-assemble at ~300 nm pitch. They join a separately made logic-process periphery wafer to the array wafer without fine-alignment hybrid bonding.
why: Fact 7 + capital: puts ~40% of periphery on a cheaper logic wafer under/over the array. Field-assembled ACF needs far less capex than hybrid-bond tools, and the die shrinks ~20-30%.

title: Totem pole: four voltage-stacked subarrays reuse one charge packet
idea: Stack four subarrays' sense-amp domains in series like a totem pole (0.75-1.0 V, 0.5-0.75 V, 0.25-0.5 V, 0-0.25 V); charge drained from the top domain's bitlines becomes the supply current of the next, so one packet does four activations' work, with small push-pull regulators balancing the domains during wide simultaneous fetches.
why: Supply energy per activation drops ~4x from charge reuse and swing is 0.25 V instead of 1 V, ~10x combined, but only if offset-trimmed SAs can sense the smaller stored signal.

title: Bootstrapped wordline drivers revive 1980s self-boost, shrinking pumps
idea: Use per-driver-group MOS bootstrap capacitors to self-boost the wordline above VDD at activation, as early NMOS DRAMs did, so only a tiny VPP pump remains to hold leakage.
why: Voltage floor and periphery (facts 10, 7): removes most charge-pump area and energy (~3-5% of die and a notable share of activation power).

title: Per-bank TTL timers replace the refresh scheduler
idea: Swap the 64 ms refresh clock for allocation lifetimes: host allocations carry a time-to-live, each bank's periphery holds a countdown timer instead of refresh counters, and on expiry the bank's data is declared dead and the bank power-gated; TTLs are capped below the bank's certified retention.
why: Zero refresh power and simpler periphery (facts 3, 7); fits network buffers, KV caches and step-scoped tensors that make up most AI memory traffic.

title: Shared oxide preamp in capacitor layer per eight cells
idea: Place one vertical IGZO or poly-Si source-follower in the BEOL capacitor layer for every 8 stacked-capacitor cells: the selected cell dumps charge onto a ~1 fF local node instead of a 60-80 fF bitline, and the preamp drives the long bitline. This combines plain 1T1C storage with gain-cell-style amplification at the cell-group level, not per cell.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): ~10x better transfer ratio lets Cs fall from 5 fF to ~1 fF and capacitor aspect ratio from ~70:1 to ~15:1, a large etch and capex relief.

title: AMOLED threshold-compensation sense amp on glass
idea: Borrowed from AMOLED 7T1C pixel compensation: in each IGZO or LTPS sense amp on a glass panel, the input transistors are first diode-connected so their own threshold is stored on a gate capacitor, then the bitline signal is applied on top, cancelling +/-300 mV thin-film threshold scatter.
why: Makes thin-film periphery on glass usable at ~30-50 mV margins, unlocking memory on Gen 8.5 panels (~60x a 300 mm wafer's area per substrate) with no EUV and no silicon.

title: Merchant-foundry periphery wafers bonded to array-only DRAM wafers
idea: Substitute DRAM-process periphery with periphery made on depreciated 28/22 nm merchant-foundry logic lines and wafer-bonded to array-only wafers. DRAM fabs then spend all their EUV and DRAM-specific tool time on cell arrays, and periphery is bought by the wafer.
why: Capital intensity and capacity: with periphery at ~49% of die, array-only wafers yield ~1.8x more bits per DRAM-fab wafer start; idle mature-node US foundry capacity becomes DRAM supply.

title: Po: grade chips like diamonds — per-bank sense-margin timing
idea: Po: memory graded stone by stone. At test, measure sense margin and retention per bank and write per-bank tRCD/tRAS/tREFI tables into SPD; controllers run each bank at its own timing, so dies that miss a single global spec on a few banks are sold instead of scrapped.
why: Usable supply: recovers ~5-10% of dies that fail global bins and gives ~15% average latency gain on strong banks with no fab change.

title: No charge pumps: neighbor-wordline bootstrap boosts selected wordline
idea: Limit: no VPP charge pumps on the die. Local wordline drivers self-boost: a precharged, deselected neighbor segment's capacitance is coupled through a MIM capacitor to kick the selected wordline from VDD to ~3 V (like NAND channel boosting), and the charge is recycled back into the neighbor when the row closes.
why: Voltage floor and periphery (facts 7, 10): deleting VPP pumps (~3-4% of the die, 30-40% conversion loss) cuts wordline energy ~30-40%.

title: Zero-temperature-coefficient bias point fixes sense timing
idea: Mobility falls and Vt drops with temperature, and at one gate overdrive the two effects cancel (the ZTC point). Bias SA enable and timing replicas at ZTC so sense delay is flat from -40 to 125 C and timing guardbands can shrink.
why: tRCD/tRAS margins ~15-25% tighter, recovering bandwidth at hot (fact 3 bandwidth loss).

title: N: nitride charge-trap self-trim cancels sense-amp mismatch
idea: Give the SA cross-coupled pair an oxide-nitride-oxide gate stack (Si3N4 from SiH2Cl2 and NH3, N2 carrier); during test a feedback loop injects hot-carrier charge into the stronger device's nitride until the pair balances, permanently trimming offset.
why: Offset below ~5 mV allows ~2x smaller SA pairs and lower Cs (facts 1, 7), using only N, H, Cl and Si process gases.

title: Impact-ionization latches sense at a 0.4 V array voltage
idea: Ideal result: CV^2 near zero because the array runs at a fraction of a volt. Build the SA cross-coupled pair from impact-ionization MOS devices whose sub-5 mV/decade switching regenerates full logic levels from a 0.4 V supply, letting VARY drop from ~1 V.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): bitline energy scales with V^2, so ~6x less array energy at 0.4 V if the cell holds enough charge.

title: Piezo-stack package clamp tunes die stress to shrink leakage tail
idea: Effect: piezo-junction effect (stress-modified bandgap and trap emission rates). A small mechanical team builds a module heat spreader with a PZT stack that applies controlled compressive stress (tens of MPa) to DRAM packages; a closed loop driven by measured retention finds the stress setpoint that minimizes trap-assisted junction leakage.
why: Refresh (fact 3): if the leakage tail shrinks 1.5-2x, the refresh interval stretches by the same factor with no die change.

title: Octopus-arm self-timed mats with replica-bitline handshakes
idea: Octopus arms run local reflex loops with little central control. Each mat generates its own sense-enable, restore-done and precharge-done events from replica bitlines (bundled-data asynchronous handshake). The bank logic sends only 'go' and receives 'done', with no worst-case global timing chains.
why: Typical mats finish 20-30% before worst-case tRCD/tRP. Self-timing raises bandwidth and cuts latency, and removes timing-generator wiring and margin (~10% of periphery power).

title: Self-timed DRAM bank with replica-bitline completion signals
idea: Inverting 'DRAM runs on worst-case clocked timings': each mat carries a replica bitline that signals when slowest-case sensing has completed, and dual-rail sense outputs drive an asynchronous handshake to the controller, removing the DLL and fixed tRCD/tRP guard bands.
why: Typical-case accesses ~20-30% faster than worst-case specs and DLL power eliminated; attacks periphery power and latency.

title: Capacitor-DAC successive approximation sense for two-bit cells
idea: Substitute the single-threshold latch with a two-step successive-approximation comparison: switched trim capacitors on the reference bitline act as a capacitive DAC that steps the reference to resolve four stored charge levels, so each cell holds 2 bits.
why: Density and cost per bit: ~2x bits per cell area if sense resolution reaches ~25 mV steps, which is helped by soft-decision ECC.

title: Telescope-mirror peel-off polymer: dry particle capture film
idea: Observatories clean mirrors with a peel-off polymer that cures around dust and lifts it away. Spin a strippable polymer onto periphery wafers after CMP or etch, let it encapsulate particles and residues, then peel it off with an adhesive roller tape in a dry module, leaving the surface clean.
why: Water: replaces post-CMP and pre-deposition brush/megasonic rinses in periphery modules (~10x less UPW per clean); the risk is complete release from trenches.

title: Micro-ring modulators driven directly from sense-amp row skip SerDes
idea: Effect: electro-optic refractive-index modulation (Pockels in thin-film LiNbO3, or carrier plasma dispersion in Si). Put micro-ring modulators at the column-select outputs so each sense-amp group modulates its own WDM wavelength; light carries the page off-die in parallel, eliminating the serializer, DLL and long global data lines.
why: Data movement (fact 5) and periphery (fact 7): I/O energy falls from 3-20 pJ/bit to <1 pJ/bit, and ~10% of die area (I/O plus DLL) is removed.

title: Time-interleaved high-speed sense amp serves eight bitlines
idea: Box: stacked cap x Si access x ADC-style time interleaving x analog mux plus isolation x bulk Si x FinFET periphery. After charge sharing, eight bitlines are isolated and hold their signals on their own parasitic capacitance while one fast, well-matched SA resolves them in ~1 ns slots through an analog mux and restores each in turn.
why: SA count /8 and SA stripe -60%; one large matched SA also lowers offset.

title: Electrochromic BIST pads let cameras read wafer test without probe cards
idea: Effect: electrochromism. Each die's built-in self-test drives a small WO3 electrochromic pad (H+ or Li+ intercalation) that turns dark blue when a mat or bank fails. A full-wafer membrane supplies only power and a few control pins, and a camera reads the pass/fail map of every die on the wafer in seconds, so no dense signal probe cards or tester channels are needed.
why: Capital intensity (fact 4): test equipment (testers, probe cards, long retention tests) is ~10-15% of cost; massively parallel optical readout could cut tester capex several-fold.
